headings.title: The Role of Evaluation in the Nursing Process
headings.content: Evaluation is the final, ongoing step of the nursing process where you judge whether your nursing actions achieved the goals you set for the patient. Without evaluation, care remains a blind guess rather than a targeted intervention. You look closely at the patient's current clinical state and compare it against the original baseline data collected during admission. This phase determines if the patient is improving, staying the same, or getting worse. In busy Nigerian hospital wards, it is easy to skip formal evaluation due to staff shortages, but taking a moment to assess the impact of care prevents complications from slipping through unnoticed.

headings.title: Comparing Patient Outcomes with Expected Goals
headings.content: When evaluating care, you measure actual patient outcomes directly against the behavioral goals or expected outcomes formulated during the planning stage. An outcome is met if the patient achieves the target behavior or physiological parameter within the specified timeframe. If the goal is partially met, progress is happening, but more time or adjusted support is required. When an outcome is completely unmet, it signals that either the diagnosis was inaccurate, the intervention was ineffective, or outside barriers interfered with healing. Documenting these specific comparisons provides a clear picture of clinical progress.

headings.title: Modifying the Care Plan Based on Findings
headings.content: Evaluation naturally drives revision. If your assessment shows that a patient is not meeting expected outcomes, you must modify the care plan immediately. Modification involves altering nursing diagnoses, adjusting target timelines, or introducing entirely new interventions. For example, if a pregnant woman with gestational hypertension shows rising blood pressure despite rest, the care plan must change to include stricter monitoring and medical consultation. Stubbornly sticking to a failing care plan compromises patient safety and delays recovery.

headings.title: Principles of Accurate Nursing Documentation
headings.content: Documentation is the written proof of the care you provide. Good charting must be factual, objective, accurate, and timely. Avoid vague terms like 'patient had a good night' or 'moderate bleeding'; instead, write measurable facts such as 'lochia rubra, approximately 50ml on pad, no clots observed.' Always chart your own care immediately after performing it, never before. Pre-charting is a dangerous professional malpractice habit that puts your license at risk. If you make a mistake on paper, draw a single neat line through it, write 'corrected by' alongside your signature, and never use correction fluid.

headings.title: Legal and Ethical Implications of Charting
headings.content: Your clinical chart is a legal document that can be subpoenaed in a court of law during malpractice lawsuits or disciplinary hearings. The golden rule of legal charting states: 'If it was not charted, it was not done.' Courts will not accept verbal claims that you performed a vital assessment if your signature is missing from the observation chart. Ethically, accurate charting respects the patient right to truthful health information and ensures continuity of care among multidisciplinary team members. Falsifying records or omitting critical data is both professional misconduct and a violation of nursing ethics.

headings.title: Evaluation and Documentation in Clinical Practice
headings.content: Putting evaluation and documentation together in everyday ward routines ensures holistic, accountable midwifery care. When attending to pregnant women in labor or postpartum mothers, your assessment leads straight into documentation, which then prompts your next evaluation cycle. Whether using traditional paper charts or emerging electronic health records, consistency remains key. Clear handover reports depend entirely on the quality of the notes you leave behind. By maintaining high standards of documentation, you protect your patients, safeguard your nursing license, and strengthen the entire healthcare team.
